meaning.evidence: Every step and quantity kept, with metric added as colour: "Preheat the oven to 425°F (220°C)", "Leave it to cool for 5 minutes in the pan before serving."

sense.evidence: Local swaps all fit: "self-raising cornmeal", "full-cream milk", "baking tin", "damp tea towel", "a quick, simple feed (even brekkie)".

authenticity.evidence: Natural Australian kitchen English: "whack it in the oven to heat", "pop it in the oven", "give it a coat of spray oil".

register.evidence: Localised but mostly plain recipe prose ("Stir in the cornmeal and mix till it's just wet through."), noticeably lighter than a level-4 brief.

tone.evidence: Keeps the friendly, practical recipe tone: "Be careful not to overmix it."

flow.evidence: Reads cleanly: "Bake till the crust is a light golden brown and a toothpick poked into the centre comes out clean."

variety.evidence: Varied where it uses slang ("whack it", "pop it", "tucking in"), though there is little of it.

essence.evidence: Unmistakably the Wikibooks recipe, structure and notes intact.

problems.original: Stir in the cornmeal and mix until just moistened.
problems.why: Typical of the plain register: the text sits lighter than level 4.

A.summary: A clean, well-localised recipe with natural Aussie touches, but well short of level 4.

meaning.evidence: Essentially the original with spelling and kitchen-word swaps; nothing lost: "Preheat the oven to 425°F."

sense.evidence: The few swaps fit: "self-raising corn meal", "full-cream milk", "frying pan", "baking tin", "fridge".

authenticity.evidence: What little there is is natural ("whack it in the oven to heat"), but US forms remain: "coat with a non-stick spray", "Assorted measuring cups", "storage bags".

register.evidence: Almost untranslated for a level-4 brief: "It is easy to make and is usually served as the bread portion of lunch or tea (supper)."

tone.evidence: The recipe's neutral instructional tone is intact, since it is mostly the original.

flow.evidence: Reads like the original, with one jarring swap in the clipped style: "If using cast-iron frying pan, whack it in the oven to heat."

variety.evidence: Almost no slang to vary; "whack it" is the lone colloquialism.

problems.quote: It is easy to make and is usually served as the bread portion of lunch or tea (supper).
problems.original: It is easy to make and is usually served as the bread portion of lunch or dinner (supper).
problems.why: Left largely untranslated, far below the level-4 brief.

problems.quote: If using cast-iron frying pan, whack it in the oven to heat.
problems.original: If using cast-iron skillet, place it in the oven to heat.
problems.why: A lone slang verb in clipped recipe-speak jars.

B.summary: Essentially the original with a few localisations; far too light for level 4.

meaning.evidence: Every step and quantity kept, but the opening overstates: "right across the Southeastern United States they serve the stuff with just about everything" (the original says it is served as the bread of lunch or dinner), and "no sugar in it whatsoever" pushes "unsweetened".

sense.evidence: Mostly exact ("easy as", "knock up a quick, simple feed", "getting stuck in", "Keep your mitts off it"), though "it usually rocks up as the bread with lunch" strains a people verb onto food.

authenticity.evidence: Largely a real Aussie voice ("into the oven she goes", "Each to their own, ay."), with "plenty of folks over there" leaning American and "ya won't believe this" a touch stagey.

register.evidence: A full level-4 retelling of a recipe, no swearing, within the dial: "Southern Cornbread, then."

tone.evidence: Still a usable, friendly recipe, but the narrator's ribbing of buttermilk breakfasts ("Cornbread and buttermilk for brekkie. Each to their own, ay.") adds a wry edge the neutral original lacks.

flow.evidence: Reads like someone talking you through it: "Using a frying pan or tin that isn't cast iron? Give it a good squirt of spray oil."

variety.evidence: Varied throughout: "Crank the oven up", "Whack it in", "into the oven she goes", "dish it up", "chuck it in the freezer".

essence.evidence: Unmistakably the recipe, every step and note kept.

problems.quote: they serve the stuff with just about everything
problems.original: usually served as the bread portion of lunch or dinner
problems.why: Overstates how it is served; an invented generalisation.

problems.quote: it usually rocks up as the bread with lunch
problems.original: is usually served as the bread portion of lunch
problems.why: "Rocks up" strains for food being served.

C.summary: The liveliest, most fully retold version at the right level, with small overstatements in the intro.

meaning.evidence: Steps kept, but quantities of time drift: "kept in the fridge for a few days" and "freeze it in storage bags for a few months" for "several", and the cool-down is fine; metric is not added.

sense.evidence: Terms fit: "a doddle to make", "bung it in the oven", "getting stuck into it", "don't overmix the bugger".

authenticity.evidence: Mostly natural ("bung it in the oven to heat up", "whack it in the oven"), with "some folks" leaning American and "a doddle" more British.

register.evidence: A chatty level-4-ish rewrite with dad-level swearing ("don't overmix the bugger"), though the equipment and notes stay plainer.

tone.evidence: Keeps the practical recipe tone while casual: "Let it cool for 5 minutes in the pan before you serve it up."

flow.evidence: Reads well, with one fiddly line: "If you're using a frypan that isn't cast iron, or a baking tin, give it a spray of non-stick."

variety.evidence: Varied: "dished up", "a doddle", "Crank the oven up", "bung it", "whack it", "Tip the batter".

problems.quote: kept in the fridge for a few days
problems.original: stored in the refrigerator for several days

problems.why: Keeps the US recipe heading where "Method" is the Australian norm.

D.summary: A lively, natural rewrite at about the right level, with minor drift in storage times.

meaning.evidence: All points kept, with metric conversions as colour: "Crank the oven up to 425°F (220°C)", "it'll keep in the fridge for several days".

sense.evidence: Every term fits: "a quick, simple feed", "tucking in", "whack it in the oven", "a good squirt of spray oil".

authenticity.evidence: Natural Australian voice: "Don't preheat any other sort of frying pan or baking tin, mind."

register.evidence: Chatty and Aussie throughout, slightly restrained for level 4: "The batter'll be a bit lumpy, and that's fine."

flow.evidence: Smooth, apart from a doubled word: "will even make a quick, simple feed of it now and then (brekkie, even)".

variety.evidence: Varied verbs ("Crank", "whack", "pop"), with fewer distinct touches than the liveliest version.

problems.quote: will even make a quick, simple feed of it now and then (brekkie, even)
problems.original: It is not unusual for some people to occasionally have a simple, quick meal—even breakfast—

E.summary: A clean, faithful, natural rewrite, a shade light for level 4.
